The sense is, He would not despise me for my forwardness in shewing my affections to him, as men commonly do in like cases, but would kindly accept of my Love, and return Love for it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 2. 7. & 3. 5.</ns0:note> I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>why should ye stir up,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>why,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> that ye stir not up, nor awake <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> love until he please <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This verse is here repeated again from <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2. 7. & 3. 5. where see the Explication of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 (<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 6.</ns0:note> Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this that cometh up from the wilder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">These words are repeated from <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 6. of which see the notes there. This and the next clause are the words either 1. Of the Daughters of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> or the Friends of the Bride and Bridegroom, admiring and congratulating this happy conjunction: Or 2. Of the Bridegroom, who proposeth the Question, that he may give the Answer here following.</ns0:note>, leaning upon her beloved <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which implies both great freedom and familiarity, and fervent affection, and dependance upon him. If these be the Bridegrooms words, he speaketh of himself in the third Person, which is usual in the Hebrew Language.</ns0:note>?) I raised thee up <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">When thou wast falln, and laid low, and wert dead in trespasses, and in the depth of misery, I revived thee.</ns0:note> under the apple-tree <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Under my own shadow; for she had compared him to an apple-tree, and declared, that un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the shadow of that Tree she had both delight and fruit, <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 2. 3. which is the same thing with this <ns0:hi>raising up.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>; there thy mother brought thee forth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Under that Tree, either the Universal or the Primitive Church did conceive and bring thee forth.</ns0:note>, there she brought thee forth <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> bare thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">These are undoubtedly the words of the Bride. The sense is, Let thy Mind and thy heart be constantly set upon me, let me be engraven upon the Tables of thine Heart. He seems to allude to the engraven Tablets which are frequently worn upon the Breast, and to the signet on a mans arm or hand, which men prize at a more than ordinary rate, as appears from <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 22. 24. <ns0:hi>Hag.</ns0:hi> 2. 23. and which are continually in their sight.</ns0:note>: for love <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">My Love to thee, from whence this desire proceeds.</ns0:note> is strong as death <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which conquers every living thing, and cannot be resisted nor vanquished.</ns0:note>, jealousie <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>zeal;</ns0:hi> my ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent Love to thee, which also fills me with Fears and Jealousies, lest thou shouldest bestow thine affections upon others, and cool in thy Love to me, or withdraw thy, Love from me: for true Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers are subject to these passions.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> hard.</ns0:note> cruel <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>hard,</ns0:hi> grievous and ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rible, and somtimes ready to overwhelm me, and swallow me up; and therefore have pity upon me, and do not leave me.</ns0:note> as the grave: the coals thereof <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> coals of fire <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It burns and melts my heart like fire.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>which hath</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> flame of the Lord.</ns0:note> most vehement flame.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pro. 6. 35.</ns0:note> if a man would give all the sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance of his house for love, it would utterly be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />temned <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">It is the nature of Love in general, and of my Love to thee, that it cannot be taken off, neither by Terrors and Afflictions, which are commonly signified in Scripture by <ns0:hi>waters</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>floods, Psal.</ns0:hi> 32. 6. & 42. 7. and elsewhere; nor by temptations and al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lurements. Nothing but the presence and favour of the beloved person can quiet and satisfie it. And therefore do not put me off with other things, but give me thy self, without whom, and in comparison of whom I despise all other persons and things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 We <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These are manifestly the words of the Bride, still continuing her speech. The present Church, which was that of the Jews, speaks of another future Church, which was to consist of the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles, which she calls <ns0:hi>little,</ns0:hi> because she was the younger Sister, and then scarce had a being; and she calls her her <ns0:hi>Sister,</ns0:hi> partly be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause she was so in the purpose of God, their common Father, though at present she was a stranger to him; and partly to inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate that the Gentile-Church should be admitted to the participa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the same priviledges with that of the Jews.</ns0:note> have a little sister <ns0:hi>b,</ns0:hi> and she hath no breasts <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">No grown and full Breasts, as Virgins have when they are ripe for Marriage, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16. 7. This signifies the present doleful estate of the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles, which as yet were not grown up into a Church Estate, and wanted the milk or food of Life, as for itself, so also for its Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers.</ns0:note>: what shall we do for our sister <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Teach us to know and perform our duty to them, which is to embrace them with sincere and fervent affections, to promote their coming in to Christ, and to rejoice in it, and not to envy it, and murmur at it, as the Jews did in the days of Christ, and of his A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles.</ns0:note> in the day when she shall be spoken for <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, for bringing her into the state of Matrimony: when Christ, and his Apostles, and others the first Ministers of the Gospel, who were Members of the Jewish Church, did speak and act for the conversion of the Gentiles.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:563" />9 If she <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This seems to be Christs Answer to the foregoing question of the Jewish Church concerning their Sister Church of the Gentiles, for which they were very solicitous. Christ therefore engageth himself to take care of her, and to provide for her, as the matter doth require, and as suits best with her condition. If the Gentiles when they are converted shall be like a <ns0:hi>Wall,</ns0:hi> strong and firm in Faith, stedfast against all Assaults and Temptations, for a <ns0:hi>Wall</ns0:hi> in Scripture use signifies strength, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 26. 1. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 15. 20. and else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where; <ns0:hi>We,</ns0:hi> my Father, and I, and the Holy Ghost, as the prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipal Builders, and my Ministers as workers with, and under us, <ns0:hi>will build upon her a palace of silver,</ns0:hi> will add more strength and beauty to her, will enlarge and adorn her, make her more amiable in mine Eyes, and more visible and glorious in the Eyes of the World: <ns0:hi>And if she be</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>a Door,</ns0:hi> which is weaker than a Wall, and where the Enemy doth or may break in upon her, if she be weak in Faith, and somtimes overcome by the tempter, yet we will not therefore reject and forsake her, but <ns0:hi>we will enclose</ns0:hi> or (as many o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers render the word) <ns0:hi>strengthen</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>fortifie her with Boards of cedar,</ns0:hi> which are not only beautiful, but also strong, and durable. If she be sincere, and open the door of her Heart to me, though she be weak, I will come into her, and make her stronger.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> a wall <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These seem to be the words of the Jewish Church to Christ, O Lord, by thy Grace I am what thou wouldst have my Sister to be, <ns0:hi>a Wall,</ns0:hi> and therefore do humbly beg and hope, that according to thy promise to her in that case, thou wiltst build upon me a Palace of Silver.</ns0:note>, and my breasts like towers <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Which stand out from and above the Wall, and are an ornament and defence to it. Of the Churches Breasts see before, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4. 5. & 7. 3, 7.</ns0:note>: then was I in his eyes, as one that found <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> peace.</ns0:note> favour <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">When by his Grace I was made a wall, he was well-pleased with me, and with his own workman<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship in me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A place not far from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> where <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> had, as it seems, a noble vineyard.</ns0:note>, he let out the vineyard unto keepers: every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand <ns0:hi>pieces</ns0:hi> of silver <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Whereby he signifies both the vast extent of the Vineyard which required so many keepers, and its singular fertility which afforded so great a Rent.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 My vineyard <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">My Church, which is oft compared to a vineyard, and is here opposed to <ns0:hi>Solomons<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>vineyard.</ns0:hi> It is much doubted and disputed whether this verse be spoken by Christ or by the Spouse; the first clause seems to agree best to the former, and the following clause to the latter. Possibly the difficulty may be reconciled by ascri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bing the first clause to Christ, and the latter to the Spouse: such interlocutions being familiar in this Book, and in other Writings of this kind.</ns0:note> which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> mine <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This Repetition is not idle, but very emphatical, to shew that Christ had a more eminent and special title to his Vine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yard, the Church, than <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> had to his Vineyard, because it was purchased not by his Money, but by his Blood, and because it was his, not only for the short time of this present Life, as <ns0:hi>Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mons</ns0:hi> was, but to all eternity.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> before me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Is under my own Eye and Care, and is not wholly committed to the Care and Management of o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, as <ns0:hi>Solomons</ns0:hi> was; <ns0:hi>I the Lord do keep it night and day,</ns0:hi> as we read <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 27. 3. <ns0:hi>I am with</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>to the end of the world,</ns0:hi> Mat. 28. 20.</ns0:note>: thou, O Solomon, <ns0:hi>must have</ns0:hi> a thousand <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">These are the Churches return to Christ, who is here called <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> as he was, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 9, 11. as elsewhere he is called <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi> Dost thou, O Christ, keep thine own Vineyard, which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> did not? Then surely it is meet that thou shouldst receive, and thou shalt receive as large a Revennue from thy Vineyard, as he did from his.</ns0:note>, and those that keep the fruit thereof, two hundred <ns0:hi>q.</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>p</ns0:hi> Though the chief Revennue belongeth, and is justly given to thee, yet thy Ministers, who serve thee in thy Vineyard, shall have, and are allowed by thee to receive; some encouragement for their service. See 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 7.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Thou that dwellest <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Hebrew word is of the feminine gender, which plainly sheweth that Christ speaks here to his Spouse, being about to depart from her for a season, as the next verse sheweth.</ns0:note>, in the gardens <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not in the Wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness of the World, for Believers are <ns0:hi>chosen,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>called out of the World,</ns0:hi> Joh. 15. 19. but in the Church, the Garden of God, which God hath fenced and appropriated to himself. He saith, <ns0:hi>Gardens,</ns0:hi> because of the many particular Congregations, into which the Church is divi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded.</ns0:note>, the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />panions <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The friends of the Bride and Bridegrom.</ns0:note> hearken to thy voice <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Diligently observe all thy words and carriages towards me, and all the trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />actions between thee and me.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 2. 14.</ns0:note> cause me to hear <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">When I am gone from thee, let me hear thy Prayers, and praises, and the preaching of my Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel to the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> flee away.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 22. 17, 20.</ns0:note> Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe, or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Seeing we must part for a time, make haste, O my beloved Bridegroom, and speedily finish the work which thou hast to do in the World, that so thou maist take me to thy self, that I may live in thine everlasting embraces. The words of this verse are borrow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2. 17. where they are explained.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
